Today it is rapidly shrinking due to reduced agricultural drainage flowing into it, exposing toxic dust from the lakebed that causes asthma and other respiratory diseases in surrounding communities.

Regenerative agriculture — a suite of practices including no-till farming, cover cropping, diverse crop rotations, and integrating livestock — can build soil organic matter, increase water retention, and sequester significant quantities of carbon. A comprehensive analysis found that widespread adoption of regenerative practices on just 50% of global cropland could sequester up to 1.85 billion tonnes of CO₂ annually.

The snow leopard inhabits high-altitude ecosystems across 12 countries in Central and South Asia, primarily at elevations of 3,000–5,000 meters in the Himalayas, Hindu Kush, and Altai ranges. Fewer than 6,400 snow leopards survive in the wild, threatened by poaching, retaliatory killing by livestock herders, and the shrinking of their high-altitude habitat as the climate warms.

New York City's watershed management program protects 1.5 million acres of land in the Catskill Mountains to maintain the quality of drinking water for 9 million residents — making it one of only a few large cities in the world that do not need to filter their water supply. The program, which began in the 1990s, has saved the city an estimated $10 billion in water filtration plant construction costs.

About 80% of the world's unexplored biodiversity is estimated to lie in the soil — a single teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes) than there are people on Earth. Soil biodiversity underpins all terrestrial food production and is severely threatened by intensive agriculture, chemical pollution, and compaction.

source.name: FAO State of Knowledge of Soil Biodiversity

text: The Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica absorbs about 40% of all CO₂ taken up by the world's oceans each year and plays a critical role in regulating global climate. However, as the ocean warms and freshens from melting glaciers, its capacity to absorb CO₂ is being reduced — transforming a critical carbon sink into a potentially less effective buffer against atmospheric CO₂ accumulation.

The woolly mammoth went extinct approximately 4,000 years ago — persisting on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until surprisingly recently — largely due to a combination of hunting by early humans and climate-driven habitat change at the end of the last ice age. Biotechnology company Colossal Biosciences is working to introduce mammoth traits into the Asian elephant genome by 2028 to potentially restore cold-adapted megafauna to the Arctic.

The prairie dog — a keystone species of North American grasslands — creates extensive underground burrow systems that are used by over 200 other species including burrowing owls, black-footed ferrets, and rattlesnakes. Prairie dog towns once covered 100 million acres across the Great Plains; today they cover less than 2% of their historic range due to shooting, poisoning, and agricultural conversion.

Tidal energy — generated by harnessing the kinetic energy of ocean tides — is the most predictable and reliable form of renewable energy, as tides follow known lunar cycles. The MeyGen tidal array in Scotland's Pentland Firth is the world's largest operational tidal energy project, generating power that predictably follows the 12.4-hour tidal cycle with near-100% uptime.

Dung beetles play a critical ecological role in nutrient cycling, pest control, and soil aeration — the ecosystem services provided by US dung beetles alone are estimated to be worth $380 million per year to the livestock industry by burying dung that would otherwise harbor parasites and release greenhouse gases. Widespread use of veterinary antiparasitics like ivermectin can kill dung beetles that feed on treated animal waste.

source.name: Journal of Applied Ecology Dung Beetles

text: The African continent is rifting apart along the East African Rift System — a geological process that will eventually split Africa into two landmasses over the next 50 million years. This process has already created the world's second-deepest lake, Lake Tanganyika (1,470 m), and may eventually form a new ocean basin between a smaller fragment and the larger African continent.

Constructed wetlands — engineered systems that use natural wetland processes to treat wastewater — can remove 90–95% of pollutants including nitrogen and phosphorus using plants, microbes, and natural filtration. They cost 30–50% less to build and operate than conventional treatment plants and provide additional ecosystem services such as wildlife habitat and carbon sequestration.

source.name: EPA Constructed Wetlands for Wastewater Treatment

text: The vaquita — a small porpoise native to the Gulf of California — is the world's most critically endangered marine mammal, with an estimated population of fewer than 10 individuals as of 2023. The species is being driven to extinction as bycatch in illegal gillnets set to poach the totoaba fish, whose swim bladder is illegally sold in China for alleged medicinal properties.

The concept of 'planetary boundaries' — proposed by a team led by Johan Rockström in 2009 — identifies nine Earth system processes with defined safe operating limits for humanity. By 2023, scientists assessed that six of the nine boundaries had already been transgressed, including climate change, biodiversity loss, land-system change, freshwater use, biogeochemical flows, and novel entities like chemical pollution.

The Antarctic Treaty System, signed in 1959 by 12 nations and now including 56 parties, designates Antarctica as a scientific preserve, bans military activities, and prohibits mineral resource extraction. The Protocol on Environmental Protection (1991) designates Antarctica as a 'natural reserve devoted to peace and science,' and a 50-year moratorium on mining activity cannot be lifted until 2048.

The Okavango Delta in Botswana is a unique inland delta — one of the few in the world — where a major river (the Okavango) flows into a vast inland alluvial fan in the Kalahari Desert instead of into the sea, creating a dynamic seasonal wetland of 15,000 km² that supports exceptional biodiversity including 530 bird species and the world's largest population of African wild dogs.

Microplastics have been found in the deepest layer of the atmosphere — the stratosphere — meaning plastic particles are now being transported globally and deposited far from any human source, including in the most remote wilderness areas. Scientists have detected microplastics in Pyrenean mountain snow, Arctic sea ice, and even on the summit of Mount Everest.

The Amazon River discharges approximately 20% of all fresh water entering the world's oceans — more than the next seven largest rivers combined — and its plume can be detected by satellites over 200 km offshore in the Atlantic Ocean. This freshwater plume suppresses hurricane formation over the tropical North Atlantic by stabilizing the ocean surface layer.

Battery energy storage capacity is growing exponentially, enabling greater integration of intermittent solar and wind power into electricity grids. Global grid-scale battery storage capacity exceeded 1,600 GWh by 2024, and the cost of lithium-ion battery packs fell from over $1,200/kWh in 2010 to below $100/kWh by 2024 — a 90%+ cost reduction in 14 years.

Sardines and anchovies — small, oily fish that feed on plankton near the base of the food chain — are among the most ecologically important fish in the ocean, transferring energy from plankton to larger predators including tuna, dolphins, and seabirds. Their populations fluctuate dramatically with natural climate cycles, and overfishing during population lows has caused collapses like the 1972 Peruvian anchovy crash.

Invasive lionfish (Pterois volitans), native to the Indo-Pacific, have spread through the Caribbean and US East Coast since first detected off Florida in 1985, likely from aquarium releases. With no natural predators, they have drastically reduced native reef fish populations by up to 80% on some reefs, threatening reef ecosystem function across a large region.

The Sundarbans — the world's largest mangrove forest straddling India and Bangladesh — is the only habitat on Earth where Bengal tigers live in saltwater mangroves and have learned to swim between islands to hunt. Rising sea levels and increasing cyclone intensity threaten to submerge significant portions of the Sundarbans within decades, further stressing the critically low tiger population there.

Wastewater from cities — if properly treated — represents a valuable source of recoverable resources, including energy from biogas, phosphorus for fertilizer, and reclaimed water for irrigation. Modern water resource recovery facilities can become net energy producers, generating biogas from sewage sludge through anaerobic digestion and potentially meeting 40–100% of their own electricity needs.

The Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is the keystone species of the Southern Ocean ecosystem, supporting populations of whales, seals, penguins, and albatrosses. A single individual weighs less than a gram, yet the collective biomass of Antarctic krill is estimated at 300–500 million tonnes — possibly the largest biomass of any single species on Earth.

Germany's Energiewende ('energy transition') policy aimed to simultaneously phase out nuclear power and fossil fuels in favor of renewables, with renewable energy reaching 46% of electricity generation by 2023 — up from just 6% in 2000. However, Germany's electricity prices rank among Europe's highest, illustrating the economic challenges of rapid energy system transformation.

The island of Borneo is home to the endangered sun bear — the world's smallest bear species, weighing only 25–65 kg — which plays a crucial role as a forest engineer by tearing apart rotting logs to find insects and honey, creating habitat for hundreds of other species. Sun bears are threatened by deforestation and the illegal wildlife trade.

The concept of 'environmental DNA' (eDNA) — genetic material shed by organisms into water, soil, or air — is revolutionizing biodiversity monitoring, allowing scientists to detect the presence of rare, cryptic, or invasive species without directly observing them. A single water sample from a lake can reveal dozens of vertebrate species that inhabit it through DNA traces left behind.

The 'albedo effect' — Earth's reflectivity — plays a crucial role in planetary temperature regulation. Snow and ice reflect up to 90% of incoming solar energy, while dark ocean water absorbs over 94%. As Arctic sea ice melts, exposing darker ocean, an amplifying feedback loop occurs: less reflective surface → more warming → more ice melt → even less reflective surface, further accelerating warming.

Africa's Sahara Desert — the world's largest hot desert at 9.2 million km² — is not static: satellite data shows it has expanded by about 10% since 1920, partly due to climate change reducing rainfall at its southern margins. However, the Sahel region south of the Sahara has also seen a 'greening' trend since the 1980s in some areas, driven by increased rainfall and deliberate reforestation.

The Mariana Trench, the deepest ocean trench at 11,034 m, is a biologically rich environment despite crushing pressure and near-freezing temperatures. The first human descent to the Challenger Deep (the deepest point) was made by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in 1960; in 2019, Victor Vescovo descended to 10,928 m, discovering new species of amphipods — and plastic pollution — at the bottom.

Offshore wind farms in the North Sea are creating unexpected marine reserves: the physical turbine infrastructure creates artificial reef habitat for fish, invertebrates, and seabirds, while fishing exclusion zones around turbines allow seafloor habitats to recover. Some studies show fish biomass inside offshore wind farm exclusion zones is 3–11 times higher than in adjacent fished areas.

The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System, completed in 1977, carries oil 1,300 km from Prudhoe Bay to the port of Valdez across permafrost terrain — and was engineered with refrigerated supports to prevent the oil's heat from thawing the permafrost and causing the pipeline to sink. As climate warming accelerates permafrost thaw across Alaska, infrastructure across the state faces billions in damage costs.

The Amazon River basin produces approximately 20% of all the fresh water that flows into the world's oceans, and this massive discharge of nutrients fuels a 'river in the sky' — atmospheric rivers of moisture that bring rainfall to southeastern Brazil and even regions as far away as the Río de la Plata basin 3,000 km to the south. Continued Amazon deforestation threatens to disrupt these moisture flows.

The black-footed ferret was declared extinct in the wild in 1979, only to be rediscovered in Wyoming in 1981 when a dog brought one home. A captive breeding program was established with 18 survivors; today, approximately 300 wild ferrets exist across the US, Canada, and Mexico through ongoing reintroduction efforts — making it one of the most successful Endangered Species Act recovery stories.

Geothermal energy provides both heating and cooling: heat pumps can extract heat from shallow ground (which maintains a nearly constant 10–16°C year-round) to heat buildings in winter, then reverse the process to cool buildings in summer. Ground-source heat pumps are 3–5 times more efficient than conventional heating and cooling systems, representing one of the most effective technologies for building decarbonization.

India has the third-largest road network in the world, and road construction through forests and wildlife corridors has fragmented habitat for tigers, elephants, and other megafauna. To address this, India has built over 50 wildlife underpasses and overpasses on highways, with camera-trap studies confirming that tigers, leopards, and elephants regularly use these crossings.

source.name: Wildlife Institute of India Road Crossing Structures

text: The Atlantic Forest of Brazil — once covering 1.3 million km² along Brazil's coast — has been reduced to only 12–15% of its original extent, making it one of the world's most threatened and most biodiverse biomes. Despite massive fragmentation, it still harbors 40% of all plant species in Brazil, 264 endemic bird species, and the golden lion tamarin, all in a heavily human-dominated landscape.

The global insect population has declined by nearly 30% over the last 30 years in many monitored regions, with some long-term studies finding biomass losses of 75% or more in German nature reserves. Insects — which make up over 70% of all animal species — are critical for pollination, decomposition, pest control, and as food for higher animals, making their decline an existential threat to terrestrial ecosystems.

The Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland (150,000–195,000 km²) straddling Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay, suffered its worst recorded wildfire season in 2020, when fires burned approximately 28% of the entire biome in a single year. The fires were driven by an extreme drought that coincided with expanded cattle ranching and deliberate burning.

Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) — native to South America — has become one of the world's most damaging aquatic invasive plants, forming impenetrable mats on lakes and rivers that block sunlight, deplete oxygen, clog water intake structures, and impede navigation. However, research has shown it can be harvested and converted to biogas, fertilizer, and biomaterial, turning an ecological menace into a resource.

The stratospheric ozone layer over the Arctic has experienced severe springtime depletion events, with a record ozone hole forming over the Arctic in spring 2020 — driven by an unusually prolonged polar vortex combined with ozone-depleting substances still present in the atmosphere from past industrial use. This contrasts with the Antarctic ozone hole, which forms more regularly each spring.

Earthworms — Charles Darwin's 'unsung heroes' of agriculture — process enormous quantities of organic matter, improving soil structure, water retention, and nutrient availability. A healthy agricultural soil may contain up to 3 million earthworms per hectare, collectively processing the entire A horizon of soil every 10–20 years. Pesticide overuse, compaction, and monoculture farming are causing earthworm population declines globally.

The concept of 'payment for ecosystem services' (PES) compensates landowners for conserving forests, wetlands, and other natural habitats that provide public benefits such as clean water, carbon storage, and flood protection. Costa Rica's national PES program, begun in 1997, has paid over $500 million to landowners for forest conservation and is widely cited as a model for combining economic incentives with conservation goals.

source.name: FAO Payment for Ecosystem Services Costa Rica

text: The Great Rift Valley runs 6,000 km from Syria to Mozambique and contains some of the world's most important freshwater lakes, including Lake Malawi, which harbors over 1,000 fish species — more than any other lake on Earth and representing about 15% of all known freshwater fish species. Most of these are cichlid fish that evolved explosively within the lake over the past million years.

Nitrogen deposition — the 'fertilization' of ecosystems by reactive nitrogen from agricultural emissions and combustion — is fundamentally altering species composition in grasslands and heathlands across Europe and North America. By favoring fast-growing grasses and weeds over slow-growing nitrogen-sensitive wildflowers, atmospheric nitrogen deposition has reduced plant diversity in European grasslands by up to 50% over 50 years.

Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous nation, is home to the largest area of tropical peatland in Asia, containing approximately 65 billion tonnes of stored carbon. Large-scale peatland drainage and burning for palm oil plantations has made Indonesia one of the world's top greenhouse gas emitters in years when major peat fires occur.

Urban rewilding — intentionally introducing wildlife and natural processes into cities — has gained traction as an approach to restore urban biodiversity and improve human well-being. London, which has declared itself the world's first 'National Park City,' has encouraged initiatives including wild-flower meadows on road verges, urban fox monitoring, and peregrine falcon nest boxes on tall buildings.

The permafrost region of Siberia contains vast quantities of ancient organic carbon in 'Yedoma' — a type of frozen loess deposited during the last ice age that contains up to 5% organic carbon by weight. When Yedoma thaws, the very rapid microbial decomposition of this ancient carbon can release enormous quantities of CO₂ and methane — Siberian Yedoma may contain 30–50 billion tonnes of labile carbon.

Restoration of natural vegetation to degraded lands has enormous potential to mitigate climate change: a 2019 study in Science estimated that restoring trees to the 0.9 billion hectares of land capable of supporting forest (excluding existing forests, agriculture, and cities) could sequester up to 205 billion tonnes of carbon — about two-thirds of all carbon released by human activities since the Industrial Revolution.

The 'sixth mass extinction' — in which vertebrate species are disappearing at a rate estimated to be 100–1,000 times the natural background rate — is the first extinction event driven by a single species (Homo sapiens). The previous five mass extinctions were caused by extraterrestrial impacts or massive volcanic eruptions, and each took millions of years for biodiversity to recover.

The Yamal Peninsula in northwestern Siberia has experienced dramatic permafrost thaw, resulting in the formation of giant craters — some over 30 meters wide and 70 meters deep — caused by the explosive release of methane gas trapped beneath the permafrost. Over 7,000 gas-filled subsurface pingos have been identified in the region that could potentially explode as permafrost continues to thaw.

The emerald ash borer — a beetle native to Asia — was accidentally introduced to North America in wooden packaging materials around 2002 and has since killed tens of millions of ash trees in the United States and Canada. Its spread represents one of the most destructive invasive forest insect events in North American history, causing billions in damage to urban forests and timber industries.

Night sky tourism — or 'astrotourism' — is a growing industry valued at $3 billion annually that depends on dark skies free from light pollution. There are now 195 International Dark Sky Places designated globally by the International Dark-Sky Association, including Exmoor National Park in England, Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand, and Big Bend in Texas.

Fog collection systems — designed to harvest water from atmospheric fog — are providing clean water in coastal and mountainous communities in Chile, Peru, Morocco, Eritrea, and elsewhere where conventional water sources are scarce. One large fog collection installation in Chile harvests 6,000 liters of water per day from coastal fog, enough to supply 330 people.

The decline of large carnivores globally — including lions, wolves, sharks, and large raptors — is releasing mesopredators (medium-sized predators) from population control in a process called 'mesopredator release.' Coyotes, raccoons, and foxes have exploded in numbers where wolves and mountain lions have been extirpated, driving declines in songbirds, small mammals, and invertebrates across North American landscapes.

source.name: Science Large Predators and Mesopredator Release

text: Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) — adding crushed alkaline minerals such as olivine or basalt to seawater — is a proposed method to accelerate ocean carbon uptake and combat acidification simultaneously. When alkaline material dissolves in the ocean, it increases the ocean's capacity to absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere; researchers estimate the technique could theoretically sequester 1–10 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year.

Whales are powerful carbon sinks: a single great whale sequesters an average of 33 tonnes of CO₂ over its lifetime by transporting carbon from surface waters to the deep ocean when it dies and sinks (the 'whale pump'). Rebuilding whale populations to pre-whaling levels could sequester up to 1.7 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year — comparable to planting 1.7 billion trees.

The global cement industry produces approximately 8% of all CO₂ emissions — more than any other industrial material. About 40% of cement's emissions come from burning fuel to heat kilns, but 60% comes from the chemical process of calcination, in which limestone (CaCO₃) is converted to lime (CaO) — making even 'green energy' powered cement kilns still major emitters without process changes.

Rewetting drained peatlands is one of the most cost-effective climate mitigation strategies available: drained peatlands emit approximately 1.9 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per year — nearly 5% of all human-caused greenhouse gas emissions — while restored peat can resequester carbon within years. The Netherlands and Germany are actively rewetting formerly drained peatlands to meet climate commitments.

The Tibetan Plateau — called the 'Third Pole' — holds the largest reserves of fresh water outside the polar ice caps, stored in approximately 46,000 glaciers and high-altitude lakes. It is the source of 10 major Asian rivers including the Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong, Brahmaputra, Ganges, and Indus, providing water to nearly 2 billion people. These glaciers are melting at an accelerating rate.

The Sargasso Sea — a region of the North Atlantic unique in being bounded by ocean currents rather than land — is the only sea without a coastline and the only place in the world where European eels go to spawn. Floating mats of Sargassum seaweed provide critical nursery habitat for sea turtles, flying fish, and juvenile blue marlin, but the ecosystem is increasingly stressed by warming waters and pollution.

Air travel is responsible for approximately 2.5% of global CO₂ emissions, but when the warming effects of non-CO₂ climate forcings such as contrail cirrus and nitrogen oxide emissions are included, aviation's total climate impact is estimated at 3.5–5% of global warming. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF), which can be made from agricultural waste or via direct air capture, could reduce aviation's lifecycle emissions by up to 80%.

The world's population of vertebrates has declined by an average of 69% since 1970, according to WWF's Living Planet Index — one of the most comprehensive measures of biodiversity loss. Freshwater species have fared worst, with freshwater vertebrate populations declining by an average of 83% over the same period, due to pollution, dams, water extraction, and invasive species.

Rewilding Europe — a continent-wide initiative to restore wildlife to degraded European landscapes — has reintroduced European bison (wisent) to Romania, lynx to Scotland, and wolverines to Sweden, while natural processes have allowed brown bears to recolonize Italy and wolves to return to Germany, France, and Denmark. Europe's large mammal populations have broadly increased since the 1960s due to rural land abandonment and protection.

The concept of 'safe and just Earth system boundaries' expands planetary boundaries by adding equity dimensions, recognizing that safe boundaries alone are insufficient if billions of people remain without access to clean water, food, or energy. A 2023 study found that current human activities breach safe boundaries for all six Earth system processes studied, while over 1 billion people still lack access to basic resource needs.

source.name: Nature Safe and Just Earth System Boundaries

text: Ethiopia planted over 350 million trees in a single day on July 29, 2019, as part of its Green Legacy Initiative aiming to plant 20 billion trees by 2022 — a world record for trees planted in 24 hours. The initiative is designed to combat deforestation that has reduced Ethiopia's forest cover from 40% a century ago to under 5% today.

The Ganges basin is home to over 400 million people — one of the most densely populated river basins on Earth — and relies heavily on Himalayan glacial meltwater and monsoon rains for its flow. Under climate change projections, initial increases in glacial melt will be followed by a 'peak water' point after which glacial runoff declines sharply, threatening water availability for agriculture and cities.

The glass eel harvest — the catching of juvenile eels as they migrate from the Sargasso Sea to European rivers — has declined by over 95% since the 1980s, bringing European eel populations to critically endangered status. European eels have one of the most remarkable life histories of any fish, migrating 6,000 km from European rivers to spawn in the Sargasso Sea, a journey no adult eel has ever been observed completing.

Kelp forests — dense underwater forests of giant kelp growing up to 60 cm per day in cold, nutrient-rich coastal waters — are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth and provide habitat for over 1,000 species of plants and animals. Sea urchin population explosions, driven by the loss of sea otters and sea stars to disease and warming, have devastated kelp forests off California and other coasts.

The Amazon's 'dieback' tipping point — at which deforestation and climate change combine to replace the rainforest with savanna — may be closer than previously thought. Some climate scientists estimate the eastern Amazon has already begun transitioning toward a drier, less resilient state after approximately 17% of the total forest was cleared, dangerously close to the 20–25% threshold proposed as the tipping point.

Traditional fishing communities in the Philippines pioneered the 'Fish Forever' model of marine conservation, establishing locally managed marine areas (LMMAs) governed by village councils with fishing rights over their adjacent coastal waters. This community-based approach has spread to over 1,700 communities across the Philippines, dramatically improving reef health and fish catch in participating villages.

The concept of 'biocultural diversity' recognizes the deep connections between linguistic, cultural, and biological diversity — communities with unique languages and cultural practices have often evolved specialized ecological knowledge that helps manage local biodiversity. Of the 6,000+ languages spoken worldwide, over 70% are concentrated in 25 biodiversity hotspots, and language extinction often accompanies biodiversity loss.

The first legally binding international plastics treaty is under negotiation through the UN Environment Programme, with member states aiming to complete it by the end of 2025. If agreed, it would set targets for reducing plastic production, eliminating problematic plastic products, and improving waste management globally — the most significant international environmental treaty since the Paris Agreement.

The California Current upwelling system along the US West Coast is one of the world's most productive ocean ecosystems, where cold, nutrient-rich water wells up from depth to support massive populations of sardines, anchovies, salmon, seabirds, whales, and sea lions. Ocean warming and acidification are disrupting this upwelling, reducing food availability for the entire food web from fish to orca whales.

The concept of 'nature-based solutions' (NbS) — using natural and semi-natural ecosystems to address societal challenges like climate change, food security, and disaster risk — is gaining traction in international policy. Protecting and restoring coastal mangroves, for example, provides a 'triple benefit': storing 5 times more carbon than tropical forests per unit area, providing nursery habitat for fish, and offering coastal protection from storm surges.

The critically endangered Javan rhino, the rarest large mammal on Earth, now survives only in Ujung Kulon National Park in Java, Indonesia, with fewer than 80 individuals remaining. This single population is highly vulnerable to disease, genetic inbreeding, and the threat of a tsunami from the nearby Anak Krakatau volcano, making conservation management extraordinarily challenging.

The 'Haliade-X' offshore wind turbine — one of the world's largest — stands 260 meters tall with blades spanning 220 meters in diameter, and can generate 13–16 MW of power per turbine. A single rotation of this turbine's blades generates enough electricity to power an average US household for one to two days.

Blue-green algae blooms (cyanobacteria) are increasing in lakes, rivers, and coastal waters worldwide due to nutrient runoff and warming temperatures. These blooms can produce toxins lethal to fish, pets, livestock, and humans; in 2019, harmful algal bloom events were reported in all 50 US states for the first time, while Lake Erie — which supplies drinking water to 11 million people — experienced massive blooms covering over 2,000 km².

The Swedish concept of 'friluftsliv' (literally 'open air life') embodies a cultural tradition of spending time in nature that is codified in Swedish law through the 'allemansrätten' (right to roam), which grants everyone the right to walk, camp, and forage on any land regardless of ownership. Research consistently finds that regular exposure to green space reduces stress, lowers blood pressure, and improves mental health.

Mining for rare earth elements and lithium — critical for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and smartphones — has severe local environmental impacts including acid drainage, radioactive waste, and water contamination. Lithium extraction from Andean salt flats (salares) in Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina threatens fragile high-altitude wetland ecosystems that are the primary breeding habitat for three flamingo species.

The mass coral bleaching event of 2023–2024 — driven by record-breaking ocean temperatures — became the fourth global bleaching event ever recorded and the most geographically extensive, affecting 54% of coral reef areas worldwide, including reefs in the Red Sea, Western Indian Ocean, Persian Gulf, and Caribbean that had previously been considered resilient to bleaching.

source.name: NOAA Coral Reef Watch Global Bleaching 2024

text: The 'Earthshot Prize' — created by Prince William in 2020 and inspired by JFK's moonshot — awards five annual prizes of £1 million each to innovators developing solutions to environmental crises across five themes: protect nature, clean our air, revive our oceans, build a waste-free world, and fix our climate. The prize aims to create 50 solutions to Earth's greatest environmental challenges by 2030.

Ecoacoustics — the scientific study of soundscapes to assess ecosystem health — has revealed that diverse, vibrant soundscapes are accurate indicators of high biodiversity, while degraded ecosystems produce impoverished acoustic environments. Bernie Krause, a pioneer of soundscape ecology, has recorded over 45% of his 5,000 recorded habitats as now silenced or gravely impaired compared to earlier recordings.

Forest bathing — 'Shinrin-yoku' in Japanese — is a health practice of spending mindful time in forests, supported by scientific research showing measurable physiological benefits. Studies find that 2-hour forest walks decrease cortisol levels by 12%, lower blood pressure by 1.9%, reduce heart rate, and increase natural killer cell activity by up to 50% — lasting several days after the walk.

source.name: International Society of Nature and Forest Medicine

text: The Sahara Desert was once a savanna teeming with wildlife — including hippos, elephants, crocodiles, and humans — during the 'Green Sahara' period roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago, when a shift in Earth's orbital parameters brought monsoon rains much further north than today. Cave paintings in the Sahara's Tassili n'Ajjer plateau depict swimmers, cattle herders, and a diverse fauna that has completely vanished.

Vultures — nature's undertakers — provide a free ecosystem service of enormous public health value by consuming carcasses and thereby preventing the spread of rabies, anthrax, and other diseases. The catastrophic crash of vulture populations across South Asia in the 1990s (caused by veterinary use of the anti-inflammatory drug diclofenac, lethal to vultures) led to population explosions of feral dogs and estimated healthcare costs of $34 billion over 15 years.

Fish farming (aquaculture) now produces more than half of all fish consumed by humans globally — a milestone crossed in 2014 — and is the fastest-growing food production sector in the world. While aquaculture reduces pressure on wild fisheries, intensive fish farming in net pens generates water pollution, disease outbreaks that spread to wild fish, and escapes of farmed fish that can hybridize with and outcompete wild populations.

source.name: FAO State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2022

text: The Amazon River contains approximately 3,000 species of freshwater fish — more than the entire North Atlantic Ocean — including the arapaima, one of the world's largest freshwater fish at up to 3 meters long, and the electric eel which generates 600-volt shocks. Nearly 1,000 new species of plants and vertebrates were discovered in the Amazon basin between 1999 and 2019, averaging one new species every two days.

The global transition from fossil fuels is already displacing workers in coal mining and coal power, creating economic hardship in communities dependent on fossil fuel industries. 'Just transition' policies — which combine job training, economic diversification, and social support for affected workers and communities — are increasingly recognized as essential for building broad political support for climate action.

Tuna — among the fastest fish in the ocean, capable of sustained speeds of 70 km/h and body temperatures up to 10°C warmer than surrounding water — are warm-blooded fish that have evolved independently of most other fish lineages. The global bluefin tuna population has been reduced to less than 3% of its pre-industrial abundance due to industrial fishing, though some populations show signs of recovery under strict catch limits.

The 'planetary diet' proposed by the EAT-Lancet Commission in 2019 — a predominantly plant-based diet that allows modest amounts of animal products — could prevent 11 million premature deaths per year while also reducing food system greenhouse gas emissions by up to 49% and significantly reducing the agricultural land footprint. Achieving this shift globally would require a halving of red meat consumption and doubling of legumes, fruits, and vegetables.

Sea turtles — which have existed for over 100 million years and survived the mass extinction that killed the non-avian dinosaurs — navigate thousands of kilometers of open ocean using Earth's magnetic field to return to the exact beach where they were born, every 2–5 years. Six of the seven sea turtle species are now threatened or endangered, primarily due to bycatch, coastal development, and climate change affecting egg incubation.

The world's fastest-advancing glacier — the Jakobshavn Glacier in Greenland — was moving at 46 meters per day in 2013, discharging icebergs that contributed measurably to global sea level rise. The glacier calved the iceberg that sank the Titanic in 1912, and Greenland's ice sheet as a whole is currently losing 279 billion tonnes of ice per year.

Amazon deforestation releases not only CO₂ but also aerosol particles that suppress cloud formation and rainfall in the basin itself, creating a self-reinforcing feedback loop: less forest → less transpiration → less rainfall → drought stress → more fires and deforestation. This 'forest-rainfall feedback' means deforestation can cause droughts that kill even intact forest far from the cleared areas.

The Elwha River in Washington State saw the largest dam removal project in US history before Klamath; after two dams were removed between 2011 and 2014, salmon returned within weeks, river sediment reconnected to the coast rebuilding beaches, and riparian vegetation began recovering rapidly. The project demonstrated that river ecosystems can recover with remarkable speed when barriers to natural processes are removed.

source.name: National Park Service Elwha River Restoration

text: Biomagnification in marine food chains concentrates persistent organic pollutants (POPs) — including DDT, PCBs, and PFAS — to dangerous levels in top predators. Polar bears in the Arctic, despite living far from any industrial source, have among the highest body burdens of POPs of any land mammal, affecting their immune systems and reproductive success; their fat stores can concentrate PCBs 3 billion times above ambient seawater levels.

The 2019–2020 Australian 'Black Summer' wildfires burned approximately 18.6 million hectares — an area the size of Cambodia — killed an estimated 3 billion animals, and produced so much smoke that it traveled around the world and measurably affected upper atmosphere chemistry. Post-fire surveys found the fires affected habitat of 832 species of animals, including 327 species for which fires burned more than 30% of their entire global range.

Underground coal seam fires — some burning for thousands of years — are a largely invisible source of greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution. Centralia, Pennsylvania, has had an underground mine fire burning continuously since 1962, making most of the town uninhabitable. India's Jharia coalfield has had fires burning for over 100 years, covering an area of 70 km² and emitting an estimated 10–20 million tonnes of CO₂ per year.

The spotted owl controversy in the Pacific Northwest during the late 1980s and 1990s brought the conflict between old-growth forest conservation and the timber industry to national attention, ultimately leading to the 1994 Northwest Forest Plan that reduced old-growth logging by 80%. This remains one of the most significant US federal land management decisions ever made, protecting over 9.5 million hectares of federal forests.

Green hydrogen — produced by electrolysis powered by renewable electricity — produces no CO₂ during production and has enormous potential for decarbonizing heavy industry, shipping, and aviation. Chile, with some of the world's best wind and solar resources in the Atacama Desert and Patagonia, has set a target to become one of the world's top three green hydrogen exporters by 2040.

The passenger pigeon — once the most abundant bird in North America, with flocks numbering in the billions that darkened the sky for days as they passed — was driven to complete extinction in just 50 years by commercial hunting and habitat destruction. The last passenger pigeon, Martha, died in the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, serving as a symbol of how rapidly humanity can destroy even seemingly inexhaustible species.

Drought stress is making trees more susceptible to bark beetle outbreaks, which have killed hundreds of millions of trees across western North America since the late 1990s in what forest scientists call an unprecedented insect-driven tree mortality event. The pine beetle epidemic in British Columbia alone killed trees across 18 million hectares — an area larger than England — releasing carbon equivalent to five years of Canada's entire transportation sector.

source.name: Natural Resources Canada Mountain Pine Beetle

text: Lichen — symbiotic organisms composed of fungi and algae or cyanobacteria — are the dominant vegetation in arctic and alpine tundra biomes, covering about 8% of Earth's land surface. Lichens grow as slowly as 0.1–1 mm per year, fix atmospheric nitrogen, and are among the first organisms to colonize bare rock, yet they are acutely sensitive to air pollution, particularly sulfur dioxide.

The 'pollution haven hypothesis' suggests that as environmental regulations tighten in wealthy countries, polluting industries relocate to developing countries with weaker standards — effectively exporting pollution rather than eliminating it. Evidence supports this for some industries, including hazardous waste disposal and certain manufacturing processes, complicating the apparent environmental improvement in developed nations.

Redd+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation) is a UN-backed framework that compensates developing countries for conserving their forests. However, reviews have found widespread 'additionality' problems — where deforestation credits are issued for forests that were never realistically at risk of being cut — as well as 'leakage,' where protected forests displace deforestation to adjacent areas.

The world's largest desalination plant — Ras Al-Khair in Saudi Arabia — produces over 1 million cubic meters of fresh water per day from the Persian Gulf, supplying Riyadh and surrounding areas. Desalination now supplies over 70% of Saudi Arabia's drinking water and is expanding globally, though conventional reverse osmosis desalination consumes 3–10 kilowatt-hours per cubic meter — making energy cost the dominant operating expense.

The golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) of Colombia's Pacific coast is the most toxic vertebrate on Earth, with enough batrachotoxin in a single frog to kill 10–20 adult humans. Indigenous Emberá people have traditionally rubbed blowgun darts on its back to create lethal hunting weapons — giving the frog its 'poison dart' common name.

Citizen science programs — in which members of the public collect scientific data — are transforming environmental monitoring at scales impossible for professional researchers. The Christmas Bird Count organized by the National Audubon Society, running continuously since 1900, involves over 80,000 volunteers counting birds across North America every winter — generating one of the longest-running wildlife datasets in history.

Urban stormwater runoff is one of the leading causes of water quality impairment in cities worldwide, carrying pollutants including heavy metals, bacteria, oil, and nutrients from roads and rooftops into waterways. 'Green infrastructure' approaches — including rain gardens, bioswales, permeable pavement, and green roofs — can reduce stormwater runoff by 50–90% while also improving urban biodiversity and aesthetics.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report found that human-caused climate change is unequivocally contributing to extreme weather events including more intense heatwaves, heavier rainfall, more powerful tropical cyclones, and more severe droughts in some regions. The attribution science linking specific weather events to climate change has advanced dramatically since the IPCC's Fifth Assessment.

source.name: IPCC AR6 Working Group I Report

text: Pangolins — shy, scaled insectivores found in Asia and Africa — are the world's most trafficked wild mammals, with an estimated one million having been poached over the past decade for their scales (used in traditional medicine) and meat. All eight pangolin species are now threatened with extinction, and COVID-19 research suggested pangolins may serve as an intermediate host for coronaviruses.

The 'garbage enzyme' — a homemade fermented liquid made from fruit peels, sugar, and water — gained popularity in Southeast Asia as an eco-friendly cleaning agent and plant fertilizer after being promoted by Thai social activist Dr. Rosukon Poompanvong. While scientific evidence for its efficacy is limited, the practice promotes household organic waste diversion and reduces the amount of food scraps entering landfills.

Spruce beetle outbreaks in Alaska driven by climate warming have killed tens of millions of Lutz spruce trees since the 1990s, transforming vast areas of southcentral Alaska's forests into standing dead wood and fueling subsequent wildfires. This represents one of the most visible and largest insect-caused forest die-offs ever recorded in North America.

Microplastic contamination in drinking water is widespread: WHO analysis found microplastics in 93% of bottled water brands tested from 11 countries, at an average of 325 particles per liter. Tap water globally contains an estimated 1.9–4.1 microplastic particles per liter, while the bottled water vs. tap water comparison suggests packaging is a major source of plastic contamination.

The Río Negro in the Amazon basin gets its distinctive black color from humic acids dissolved from decaying plant material in the poorly-drained Amazonian lowlands. Despite its tea-dark color, the Rio Negro is one of the largest rivers in the world by discharge, and its acidity (pH 3.5–5.5) and lack of nutrients makes it surprisingly inhospitable to disease-carrying mosquitoes — a discovery that may have implications for malaria control.

The global steel industry contributes approximately 7–9% of all human CO₂ emissions, as traditional blast furnace steel production uses coking coal as both a fuel and a chemical reducing agent. 'Green steel' production using hydrogen instead of coal as a reducing agent could eliminate most of these emissions; Sweden's HYBRIT project produced the world's first hydrogen-reduced steel in 2021.

The biomass energy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) concept — burning sustainably grown biomass for energy while capturing and storing the CO₂ produced — is theorized to produce 'negative emissions.' However, many scientists warn that producing BECCS at the scale envisioned in some climate models would require more land than is available for agriculture while providing significant water stress and biodiversity loss.

Mangroves are among the most effective carbon sinks per unit area on Earth, storing three to five times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests due to the deep, waterlogged peat soils they accumulate over centuries. Global mangrove area has declined by 35% since the 1980s due to coastal aquaculture, agriculture, and development, releasing stored 'blue carbon' as CO₂.

The Saiga antelope — a critically endangered species native to the Eurasian steppes with a distinctive bulbous nose that filters cold, dry air — experienced a catastrophic mass mortality event in May 2015 when over 200,000 animals (more than 60% of the global population) died within three weeks from hemorrhagic septicemia triggered by a climate-driven combination of unusual warm and humid weather.

Scientists are using CRISPR gene-editing technology to develop disease-resistant American chestnut trees — nearly wiped out by an accidental fungal blight introduced from Asia around 1900 that killed an estimated 3–4 billion trees. The genetically engineered chestnuts carry a wheat gene that neutralizes the oxalic acid produced by the blight fungus, without affecting the tree's other characteristics.

Phosphorus — essential for all life and with no synthetic substitute — is a finite mineral that cannot be manufactured and is only found in economically recoverable concentrations in a few countries, most notably Morocco which controls roughly 70% of world reserves. Unlike nitrogen, which can be fixed from the atmosphere, phosphorus must be mined, and current agricultural waste of phosphorus threatens long-term food security.

The Bald Eagle — the symbol of the United States — was nearly extinct by the 1960s due to hunting and eggshell thinning caused by the pesticide DDT, with only 417 nesting pairs remaining in the lower 48 states by 1963. After DDT was banned in 1972 and the species was protected under the Endangered Species Act, bald eagle populations recovered to over 9,789 breeding pairs by 2006, when they were removed from the threatened species list.

Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) — deliberately releasing sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere to reflect sunlight — is one of the most discussed solar geoengineering proposals, modeled after the cooling effect of large volcanic eruptions like Pinatubo (1991) which temporarily reduced global temperatures by 0.5°C. Scientists warn that while SAI could reduce peak temperatures, terminating it abruptly would cause rapid 'termination shock' warming.

The Atlantic cod — once so abundant off Newfoundland that European explorers reported fish thick enough to walk on — was the foundation of a 500-year commercial fishery before collapsing spectacularly in 1992 when the entire Grand Banks cod population crashed to 1% of its historical level. Despite a fishing moratorium imposed that year, the northern cod stock had not fully recovered 30 years later, partly because the ecosystem had shifted to a new state dominated by shrimp and crab.

Marine heatwaves — periods of anomalously warm ocean temperatures — have doubled in frequency and increased in intensity since 1982. The 'Blob' — an unprecedented marine heatwave in the Northeast Pacific from 2013 to 2016 — warmed the Pacific Ocean by up to 6°C above normal, killing massive numbers of seabirds and marine mammals, triggering harmful algal blooms, and collapsing salmon populations.

Passive cooling technologies — including radiant cooling, natural ventilation, evaporative cooling, and earth tubes — can reduce or eliminate the need for air conditioning in many climates. A radiant cooling system recently developed using a specially engineered metamaterial panel can cool buildings below ambient air temperature using passive radiative cooling to outer space — without any electricity consumption.

Papua New Guinea contains approximately 6–8% of the world's biodiversity in just 0.5% of Earth's land area, including over 800 bird species, 300 mammal species, and 20,000 plant species. The island is home to birds of paradise — 44 species known for extraordinary male plumage and elaborate courtship dances — which naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace described as 'the most perfectly adapted beings that have ever existed.'

The Yellow River (Huang He) of China — the 'cradle of Chinese civilization' — no longer consistently reaches the sea; its lower reaches dried up completely for 226 days in 1997 due to agricultural water extraction. China has subsequently improved management through the Yellow River Water Allocation Plan, but the river still faces severe water stress from a combination of overuse, pollution, and decreased glacial runoff.

source.name: World Bank Yellow River Basin Management

text: The world's coral reefs are geologically significant structures: the Great Barrier Reef, composed of the accumulated calcium carbonate skeletons of trillions of polyps, is the largest living structure on Earth and the only one visible from space. Building the structure has taken approximately 500,000 years of continuous coral growth, accumulating limestone deposits up to 130 meters deep.

source.name: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

text: Orca (killer whale) populations are threatened by the depletion of their prey — primarily Chinook salmon in the Pacific Northwest — as well as noise pollution, chemical contamination, and vessel disturbance. Southern Resident killer whales of the Salish Sea number only 73 individuals and are critically endangered; studies show they spend up to 25% of their time in prey-searching mode, indicating chronic nutritional stress.

source.name: NOAA Southern Resident Killer Whale Recovery

text: Solar-powered irrigation is transforming smallholder agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where over 90% of agricultural land is rain-fed and dependent on increasingly variable rainfall. Solar irrigation pumps require no fuel costs, can be deployed rapidly, and enable year-round cultivation — Bangladesh alone has installed over 500,000 solar irrigation pumps serving more than 2 million farmers.

The platypus — one of only five surviving monotremes (egg-laying mammals) — uses electroreception to detect the electric fields produced by prey in murky water, allowing it to hunt with its eyes, ears, and nostrils closed. Its genome was found to contain genes related to both reptile and mammal characteristics, as well as genes for venom production, reflecting its ancient evolutionary lineage.

The 'urban metabolism' framework analyzes cities as organisms that consume resources (energy, water, food, materials) and produce waste. Studies show that compact, high-density cities with good public transit have per-capita carbon footprints 20–50% lower than sprawling low-density cities, suggesting urban planning is one of the most powerful long-term tools for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The Congo Basin's tropical forests are burning more frequently than previously measured: satellite data show that savanna fires at the edges of the rainforest are increasingly penetrating the forest interior during dry seasons, suggesting the forest is drying and becoming more vulnerable to fire — a warning sign resembling dynamics seen in the Amazon before its accelerating deforestation and fire problems.

The Western black rhinoceros was officially declared extinct by the IUCN in 2011, having been reduced from tens of thousands of individuals in the 1900s to just a handful by the 2000s, primarily due to poaching for its horn. The broader African rhino horn poaching crisis peaked in 2015 when 1,349 rhinos were killed in South Africa alone — though intensive anti-poaching measures have since reduced these numbers.

Coral 'marriage' programs are testing a breakthrough technique in which coral from different climate adaptation backgrounds are cross-bred to create thermally tolerant offspring for reef restoration. Scientists at the Australian Institute of Marine Science have successfully raised millions of thermally tolerant coral larvae that survive bleaching temperatures, offering hope that assisted evolution could help reefs survive climate change.

Plastic-eating bacteria and fungi are being discovered with increasing regularity: Ideonella sakaiensis, discovered in 2016 near a plastic bottle recycling site in Japan, can fully degrade PET plastic; meanwhile, the wax moth caterpillar's gut bacteria can break down polyethylene. Scientists are working to accelerate these biological degradation processes for industrial-scale plastic waste management.

Sperm whales are the world's largest toothed predators, diving to depths of over 2,000 meters for up to 90 minutes to hunt giant squid. They produce the loudest sounds of any animal — clicks reaching 230 decibels used for echolocation and communication — and their ambergris (a waxy substance from their intestines) was historically used as a fixative in luxury perfumes.

The 'climate grief' and 'eco-anxiety' phenomena — psychological distress caused by awareness of ecological destruction and climate change — are increasingly recognized by mental health professionals. A 2021 study of 10,000 young people in 10 countries found 59% were very or extremely worried about climate change, with 45% saying climate anxiety affected their daily functioning.

The Borneo pygmy elephant — the world's smallest elephant, standing just 2.5 meters tall — is genetically distinct from mainland Asian elephants and has likely been isolated on Borneo for 300,000 years. Only approximately 1,500 individuals remain, confined to a shrinking area of northeast Borneo that is increasingly fragmented by palm oil plantations and logging.

Environmental impact assessments (EIAs) are legal requirements in most countries before major infrastructure projects can proceed, designed to identify and mitigate harm to ecosystems, communities, and air and water quality. However, critics note that most EIA frameworks are primarily designed to inform decision-making rather than to prevent environmentally harmful projects, with 'significant harm' thresholds often set too high.

The 'Miracle of Chile' — often cited by economists as proof of free-market success — was built partly on the massive exploitation of copper deposits that make Chile the world's largest producer (30% of global supply). Copper mining in Chile consumes 7% of the country's electricity, generates enormous quantities of tailings, and has severely impacted the Atacama's water systems, raising questions about the long-term environmental costs of mineral extraction.

Extreme heat is now the deadliest weather hazard in many countries, claiming more lives than floods, hurricanes, and tornadoes combined in the United States. The 2003 European heat wave killed approximately 70,000 people, and the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome killed an estimated 1,400 people in Canada and the US, shattering temperature records by 5°C in cities unaccustomed to extreme heat.

Biogas — produced by anaerobic digestion of organic waste including food scraps, agricultural residues, and sewage — provides approximately 35 exajoules of energy globally, roughly equivalent to 1% of current global energy supply, and is growing rapidly. Countries including Sweden and Germany are pioneering the use of 'biomethane' (purified biogas) in the same gas distribution networks used for natural gas, providing a near-term decarbonization pathway for heating.

The Fossa — Madagascar's top land predator, distantly related to the mongoose — is a cryptic carnivore found only in Madagascar's diminishing forests, growing to 80 cm in body length and capable of running vertically up tree trunks. Only about 2,500 Fossa survive, threatened by the same deforestation that has eliminated 90% of Madagascar's original forest cover and driven it to be called the world's single most threatened biodiversity hotspot.

The 30x30 conservation target — protecting 30% of land and oceans by 2030 — would require protecting an additional 900 million hectares of land, an area larger than Brazil. Meeting this target using a 'nature-first' approach — prioritizing existing natural habitats, intact wilderness, and biodiversity hotspots — could protect more than 50% of the world's terrestrial species while securing critical carbon stocks.

The Monarch butterfly's multi-generational migration — spanning up to 4,800 km from Canada and the United States to their overwintering grounds in Mexican oyamel fir forests — involves up to four generations of butterflies. No individual completes the full round trip; instead, a 'super generation' that lives 8 months (compared to 6 weeks for summer generations) makes the southward journey, then their great-great-grandchildren return north.

The concept of 'polluter pays' — a fundamental principle of environmental law codified in the OECD in 1972 and in numerous national and international regulations — requires that those responsible for pollution bear the costs of prevention, control, and remediation. Despite its widespread adoption in law, externalization of pollution costs remains the norm in many sectors where regulatory enforcement is weak.

Glacier retreat is threatening the livelihoods of millions of people globally who depend on glacial meltwater for agriculture and drinking water. Bolivia's Chacaltaya Glacier — once home to the world's highest ski resort and an important water source for La Paz — completely disappeared in 2009, about 20 years ahead of schedule. Andean glaciers provide water to over 50 million people and have lost approximately 30–50% of their volume since 1950.

Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) held by Indigenous peoples often contains centuries-old insights about local ecosystems, weather patterns, and species behavior that are being validated by modern science. Inuit hunters identified changes in sea ice behavior decades before scientific monitoring detected them, and Australian Aboriginal 'fire stick farming' — burning landscapes to encourage regrowth — is now recognized as an effective way to reduce catastrophic wildfire risk.

The global supply of fish meal and fish oil — derived largely from anchovies and other small pelagic fish from the Southeast Pacific — is under pressure from both overexploitation and climate change affecting fish distribution. These products are essential for aquaculture feeds, and their depletion threatens the aquaculture industry just as it is being promoted as a sustainable alternative to capture fisheries.

The naked mole rat, a rodent that lives in underground colonies in East African savannas, is the longest-lived rodent known — some individuals survive for over 30 years compared to 2–3 years for similarly sized mice — and shows no age-related increase in cancer incidence. Research on naked mole rats' remarkable longevity and cancer resistance is informing aging and cancer biology.

Invasive species cost the global economy approximately $1.4 trillion per year — roughly 5% of global GDP — making biological invasions one of the most expensive categories of environmental damage. New Zealand, an island nation with a high proportion of endemic species, has invested heavily in invasive species control and has the world's most ambitious 'Predator Free 2050' program aiming to eradicate all invasive mammalian predators from the country.

The Caspian Sea — the world's largest inland body of water — has fallen by more than 3 meters since 1995, driven by warming temperatures that increase evaporation and reduced inflows from snow and glacier melt across Central Asia. This dramatic recession is threatening the breeding grounds of the Caspian seal, the spawning rivers of Caspian sturgeon (which produce 90% of the world's natural caviar), and coastal infrastructure across five countries.

source.name: Geophysical Research Letters Caspian Sea Level

text: Carbon pricing — either through a direct carbon tax or a cap-and-trade emissions trading system — is now in place in jurisdictions covering about 23% of global greenhouse gas emissions, with revenue from carbon pricing schemes exceeding $95 billion in 2023. Economic research consistently finds carbon pricing to be among the most cost-efficient instruments for reducing emissions, though political opposition limits its reach and price levels.

Giant clams (Tridacna gigas) — the world's largest bivalve mollusks — can live for over 100 years and grow to 1.3 meters in length and 200 kg in weight. They harbor billions of photosynthetic algae in their tissues that provide up to 90% of their nutritional needs from sunlight, making them solar-powered shellfish. Giant clams have been severely overharvested across the Indo-Pacific for food and their decorative shells.

Industrial chicken production now dominates the planet's biomass of wild birds: approximately 70% of all birds on Earth by mass are domesticated poultry, primarily chickens, while wild birds constitute only 30%. The modern broiler chicken, selectively bred to grow from egg to slaughter weight in 47 days, weighs about five times more than wild jungle fowl and would be unable to survive independently in nature.

source.name: PNAS Biomass Domestic vs Wild Birds

text: Mass coral restoration projects using 'coral gardening' — growing coral fragments on underwater nursery structures then transplanting them to degraded reefs — have shown promising results in the Caribbean and Florida Keys. The Coral Restoration Foundation has become the world's largest coral restoration organization, growing and planting over 200,000 corals annually, though scientists note that restoration alone cannot address the root causes of coral decline.

The Tibetan Antelope (chiru) — famous for its extraordinarily fine underwool called shahtoosh — was nearly driven to extinction by demand for this luxury fiber in the 1990s, when an estimated 20,000 were killed each year. International trade bans and Chinese law enforcement have allowed the population to recover from approximately 65,000 in 1999 to over 300,000 today, representing one of the most rapid recoveries of any endangered large mammal.

The Blue Economy — sustainable use of ocean resources for economic growth while preserving ocean health — is valued at approximately $3 trillion per year. Key sectors include fisheries, aquaculture, shipping, tourism, and offshore energy; 40% of the world's population lives within 100 km of a coast and is dependent in some way on ocean resources.

The 'Anthropocene' — a proposed geological epoch defined by humanity's planetary-scale impacts — has been a focus of international scientific debate since Paul Crutzen popularized the term in 2000. The Working Group on the Anthropocene proposed formally marking its beginning at around 1950, when radioactive fallout from nuclear weapons testing, synthetic pesticides, and dramatic acceleration of greenhouse gas emissions became detectable globally in sediment records.

Agrivoltaics — the co-location of solar panels and agricultural crops on the same land — can improve both energy and food production simultaneously. Studies show certain crops (including tomatoes, lettuce, and potatoes) actually perform better under partial solar panel shading, which reduces heat stress and water evaporation, while the panels generate electricity. The land-use efficiency of dual-use agrivoltaic systems is 60–70% higher than single-use alternatives.

River dolphins — four surviving species found in the Amazon, Orinoco, Ganges-Brahmaputra, and Yangtze basins — are among the world's most threatened freshwater mammals. The baiji dolphin of the Yangtze River was declared functionally extinct in 2006, becoming the first large mammal declared extinct primarily due to human activities in over 50 years; the Yangtze finless porpoise that lives alongside it is now also critically endangered.

Cloud forests — mountain forests perpetually enshrouded in mist — are among the most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems on Earth, found only at certain elevations where temperatures and humidity create the right conditions for cloud immersion. As climate change pushes cloud zones upward in elevation, cloud forests can only 'escape' by moving up the mountain until there is no more mountain — a process called 'cloud zone uplifting.'

The critically endangered Spix's macaw — a vivid blue parrot of Brazil — was declared extinct in the wild in 2019 after the last known wild individual disappeared in 2000. Some 150 individuals survive in captivity, and in 2022, eight captive-bred Spix's macaws were successfully returned to Brazil as part of a reintroduction program near Curaçá, Bahia, where habitat has been partially restored.

Terpenes — the aromatic compounds released by forests (the 'forest smell') — form organic aerosols in the atmosphere that act as condensation nuclei for cloud formation. Boreal and temperate forests effectively 'make their own rain' through this process, and large-scale deforestation can reduce regional rainfall by reducing cloud formation — adding a direct hydrological benefit to forest conservation beyond carbon sequestration.

source.name: Nature Forest Aerosols and Cloud Formation

text: The oarfish — the world's longest bony fish, reaching up to 11 meters in length — is believed to be the origin of sea serpent legends from sailors across cultures. It inhabits the mesopelagic zone at depths of 200–1,000 meters and is rarely seen alive; most knowledge of living oarfish behavior comes from rare video footage taken by deep-sea research vehicles.

In situ conservation — protecting species in their natural habitats — is complemented by ex situ conservation in zoos, botanical gardens, and seed banks. The world's botanical gardens collectively maintain over 100,000 plant species in living collections — about one-third of all known plant species — and the Millennium Seed Bank Partnership has banked seeds of over 40,000 species as insurance against extinction.

Antarctica's Lake Vostok — hidden beneath 3.7 km of ice and sealed from the surface for an estimated 15–35 million years — is one of the largest subglacial lakes on Earth, covering 15,000 km² at a depth of 800 meters. Scientists drilling into it in 2012 found microbial life in the ice just above the liquid water, raising hopes for similar life in the subsurface oceans of Jupiter's moon Europa.

The world's deep-sea fishing industry increasingly targets seamounts — underwater mountains that concentrate fish and invertebrates — with destructive bottom trawls that can flatten their fragile cold-water coral and sponge communities that took thousands of years to develop. Over 30,000 seamounts exist in the oceans; most are beyond national jurisdiction and almost entirely unprotected.

Pollen records preserved in lake sediments and peat bogs — called palynology — allow scientists to reconstruct vegetation and climate changes dating back millions of years. These pollen archives have revealed dramatic shifts in vegetation zones during past climate changes, confirming that current rates of warming are unprecedented in at least 2,000 years and demonstrating that forests can shift their ranges by hundreds of kilometers in response to climate.

Wood-wide web research has shown that trees under insect attack release volatile chemical compounds that neighboring trees detect and respond to by ramping up their own chemical defenses before being attacked. This interspecies communication — which can propagate across distances of tens of meters through both air and mycorrhizal networks — represents a form of collective immune response that has no direct parallel in other plant communities.

Floating wetlands — buoyant mats of native aquatic plants installed in lakes and reservoirs — are being used in many countries to improve water quality by absorbing excess nutrients, providing habitat for waterfowl, and cooling water temperature. They are particularly effective at removing nitrogen and phosphorus before they trigger algal blooms, and can be deployed as retrofitted nature-based solutions to existing water infrastructure.

The 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico — the largest marine oil spill in history — released approximately 4.9 million barrels of oil over 87 days, causing massive mortality of marine life and contaminating 1,000 miles of coastline. Scientists continued finding evidence of harm to deep-sea coral communities, dolphin reproduction, and fish embryo development more than a decade after the spill.

source.name: NOAA Deepwater Horizon Natural Resource Damage Assessment

text: The concept of 'circular economy' — in which materials are kept in use as long as possible through reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and recycling — could reduce global material consumption by 32% and cut greenhouse gas emissions by 22.8 billion tonnes annually by 2050. The European Union has adopted circular economy action plans, but the global economy currently only recycles about 8.6% of all materials used — the 'circularity gap.'

Scientists studying the Siberian 'zombie viruses' thawed from permafrost have successfully revived ancient viruses including Pandoravirus yedoma, with a genome of 2.5 million base pairs — the largest viral genome known — that had been frozen for 48,500 years. While the viruses revived in the lab can only infect amoebae, the discovery raises concern that thawing permafrost could release unknown ancient pathogens that modern immune systems have never encountered.

The Lena River in Russia is one of the few major rivers that drains into the Arctic Ocean, transporting enormous quantities of freshwater, sediment, and organic carbon that influence Arctic Ocean chemistry and sea ice dynamics. Satellite imagery shows the Lena Delta — one of the largest river deltas in the world — is experiencing dramatic changes as permafrost thaw increases sediment delivery and alters river channel patterns.

The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) — a critically endangered crocodilian native to the Indian subcontinent with a characteristic long, slender snout — was reduced to fewer than 200 individuals in the 1970s before conservation programs began reintroducing captive-bred animals. Its population has partially recovered but faces continued threats from sand mining, fishing nets, and pollution in Ganges and Chambal river systems.

Nuclear power, despite public perception, has the lowest lifecycle fatalities per unit of energy of any major power source, including wind and solar. A study published in The Lancet estimated that nuclear power's death rate from accidents, air pollution, and other causes is 0.07 deaths per terawatt-hour — compared to 24.6 for coal and 2.8 for natural gas — yet it generates around 10% of global electricity.

The chestnut-crowned antpitta, a secretive forest bird of the Andes, was famously trained to approach and accept worms from the hands of a ranger at a reserve in Ecuador — filmed in a viral video that dramatically changed public and scientific knowledge of its behavior. Similar 'antpitta feeders' have been established across several Ecuadorian reserves, turning formerly near-impossible-to-see birds into accessible ecotourism attractions that directly fund conservation.

The discovery of deep-sea polymetallic nodules — potato-sized rocks containing manganese, nickel, cobalt, and copper — has sparked interest in deep-sea mining as a potential source of minerals needed for clean energy technologies. However, scientists warn that deep-sea mining would destroy ancient, slow-recovery ecosystems and disturb sediment plumes over vast areas of the seabed, with impacts still poorly understood.

source.name: IUCN Deep Sea Mining Issues Brief

text: Climate migration is already occurring: rising seas, increasing droughts, and intensifying storms are displacing millions of people annually from low-lying deltas, arid regions, and small island states. The World Bank projected in 2021 that without significant climate action, 216 million people could be forced to migrate within their own countries by 2050, with the most vulnerable regions being sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America.

The Ross Sea Marine Protected Area, established in 2016 as the world's largest MPA at the time (1.55 million km²), protects one of the last nearly intact marine ecosystems on Earth and serves as a scientific reference site for studying pristine ocean food webs. The MPA was the product of 16 years of diplomatic negotiations among 25 nations and the European Union through the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources.

Geothermal energy from deep hot rock — engineered geothermal systems (EGS) that create heat-exchange reservoirs by fracturing deep rock — could theoretically provide unlimited baseload renewable electricity from virtually anywhere on Earth, since heat increases with depth everywhere. The US Department of Energy's 'Enhanced Geothermal Shot' initiative aims to reduce EGS costs by 90% by 2035 to unlock this potential.

Agroforestry — the deliberate integration of trees and shrubs into crop or livestock farming systems — is practiced on over 1 billion hectares worldwide and can increase biodiversity, store carbon, improve soil health, provide shade and wind protection for crops, and deliver additional products (fruits, timber, fodder). In West Africa, farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR) of trees on farmland has transformed degraded landscapes across millions of hectares.

The International Seabed Authority (ISA) — the UN body responsible for governing deep-sea mining in international waters — has issued exploration licenses to 31 contractors covering 1.3 million km² of the Pacific Ocean floor. The ISA is under pressure to finalize a 'Mining Code' that could allow commercial extraction to begin; scientists and environmental groups are calling for a moratorium until impacts are better understood.

Noctiluca scintillans — a bioluminescent dinoflagellate that blooms in nutrient-rich waters — creates the spectacular sea sparkle phenomenon seen on beaches where waves appear to glow blue at night. However, large Noctiluca blooms are a sign of deteriorating ocean water quality and can deplete oxygen, creating hypoxic conditions harmful to fish and invertebrates in coastal waters.

Net Zero Energy Buildings (NZEB) — buildings that generate as much energy from renewable sources (typically rooftop solar) as they consume annually — are becoming standard in advanced building codes. Denmark, Germany, and California require new public buildings to meet near-zero energy standards; the global potential of NZEB deployment could eliminate approximately 7% of global carbon emissions from buildings.

The high seas — international ocean waters beyond national jurisdiction — cover 64% of the ocean's surface and 95% of its volume, yet until 2023 were virtually ungoverned for conservation purposes. The High Seas Treaty (formally, the Agreement under UNCLOS on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction) agreed at the UN in 2023 provides the first legal framework for creating marine protected areas in international waters.

Freshwater turtles are one of the world's most endangered groups of vertebrates: approximately 68% of freshwater turtle species are threatened with extinction, more than any other group of vertebrates. They are harvested in massive quantities for food and traditional medicine, particularly for markets in China, and face additional pressure from habitat destruction and pollution.

Sandstorms from the Sahara desert deposit an estimated 27 million tonnes of Saharan dust over the Amazon basin every year — a quantity equivalent in mass to 2.8 billion baby elephants.
